title: Design and Craft
description: Ten essays, profiles and reports on design and craft: the chair as a problem, a Swiss typeface designer, doors that need no sign, the Shakers, a violin maker, the paper clip, Japanese joinery, a design exhibition, a restored farm table and a week on a bird island.

lessons.title: The Chair as a Problem
lessons.summary: An essay on why the chair, which looks like the simplest of objects, is one of the hardest to design well.
lessons.text:
Every design student is asked, sooner or later, to design a chair, and almost every student discovers that the task is harder than it looks. A chair seems the simplest of objects: a seat, four legs, perhaps a back. Yet it must hold a heavy body that never keeps the same position for long, and it must look like something a person would want to live with.

The first difficulty is the body itself. No chair suits everyone, and the designer who hopes to please people universally is soon disappointed. A seat that is perfect for a tall man leaves a short woman's feet hanging in the air. No shape has been found that is universally comfortable, only shapes that suit most people, most of the time.

Good designers therefore study the contour of the human back and legs. A seat that follows the contour of the body spreads its weight over a wide area and lessens the pressure on any one point. A gently curved back lessens the strain on the spine.

We sit because we are weary, and a well-made chair answers the weary body without fuss. The office chair goes further: it turns on a central pivot, so that a worker can face the desk, the window or a colleague without standing up. The pivot is a modest piece of steel, but it changed the way offices work.

Some designers attempt drastic solutions. They balance a person atop a large rubber ball, or atop a block of foam. A few of these drastic experiments become classics; most end up in museums, admired but rarely used. The chairs that last tend to be coherent rather than surprising. Every part has a reason, and the reasons fit together, so that the legs, the seat and the back read as one coherent idea.

There is an old way of thinking about this. The Tao Te Ching, the ancient Chinese book of the Tao, or the Way, observes that a bowl is useful because of the empty space inside it, and a room because of the space between its walls. In the spirit of the Tao, one might say that a chair, too, is defined by an absence: the space where a person will sit. The designer shapes wood and steel only in order to shape that empty space.

Seen this way, the chair is less a sculpture than a promise: a place for the body to rest. The best chairs keep that promise so quietly that we forget they are there.

Questions:
Why is it impossible to design a chair that pleases people universally?
Bodies differ, so a seat that is perfect for a tall man leaves a short woman's feet hanging in the air.
How does a seat that follows the contour of the body help the person who sits in it?
It spreads the weight over a wide area and lessens the pressure on any one point.
What does the pivot of an office chair allow a worker to do?
It allows the worker to face the desk, the window or a colleague without standing up.
What happens to most drastic experiments, such as a seat atop a rubber ball?
Most of them end up in museums, admired but rarely used.
What does the Tao Te Ching say about a bowl?
It says that a bowl is useful because of the empty space inside it.

lessons.title: Letters for a Living
lessons.summary: A profile of Margrit Hofer, a Swiss typeface designer whose ridiculed first design became her lifelong signature.
lessons.text:
In the corner of Margrit Hofer's studio in Basel stands a wooden cabinet with forty shallow drawers. Each drawer holds the drawings for one typeface, and together they record a working life of nearly fifty years. Hofer, who is now seventy-eight, still draws letters by hand before she touches a computer. "The hand knows things the screen does not," she says.

She did not set out to design type. As a girl she aspired to be a painter, and she spent two years at art school before a teacher showed her a book printed in the sixteenth century. She still remembers the shock of seeing how much feeling could live in the shape of a single letter. From then on she aspired to nothing else.

Her first typeface, finished when she was twenty-five, was met with ridicule. Swiss design at the time favored clean, strict letters without decoration, and Hofer's letters had small curling strokes that one critic compared to the leaves of a vine. He meant it as ridicule. She took it as a description. The leaf became her motif, appearing, in quieter forms, in almost everything she drew afterward. Even in her plainest typefaces, the motif survives in the tail of a letter or the curve of a comma.

For several years she worked under an alias. The company that bought her designs preferred to sell them under a man's name, and the alias it chose was Hans Brandt. Hofer laughs about it now, but she admits that the alias hurt. The company paid her 800 francs for her second typeface, roughly what a junior clerk earned in a month. Those 800 francs, she says, bought her a better lamp and a great deal of paper.

Legitimacy came slowly. A publisher of poetry chose one of her typefaces for a series of lyric poems, and readers wrote to say that the letters seemed to breathe with the lines. The lyric quality that critics had once laughed at was now the reason people wanted her work. With that legitimacy came her own name on her designs at last.

Then came the restructuring of the whole industry, when computers replaced metal type and many old companies closed or merged. During one restructuring, her early designs were discontinued, and for ten years they could not be bought at all. Hofer redrew them for the screen herself. The discontinued typefaces returned, sharper and more complete than before.

Today she turns down most requests. She says she simply has no bandwidth for large projects, and she prefers to spend what bandwidth she has on teaching. Students arrive expecting a celebrity and find a small woman with ink on her fingers who asks them to draw the same letter fifty times.

Questions:
What did Margrit Hofer aspire to be as a girl?
She aspired to be a painter.
How did a critic respond to her first typeface?
He met it with ridicule and compared her strokes to the leaves of a vine.
Why did she work under an alias?
The company that bought her designs preferred to sell them under a man's name.
How much was she paid for her second typeface?
She was paid 800 francs.
What happened to her early designs during the restructuring of the industry?
They were discontinued, and later she redrew them for the screen herself.

lessons.title: The Door That Explains Itself
lessons.summary: A short report on why a well-designed door needs no sign, and how a theater fire changed the way exit doors open.
lessons.text:
Most of us have done it: walked up to a glass door, pulled firmly on the handle, and found that the door wanted to be pushed. We blame ourselves and feel foolish. The designer Don Norman, in a famous book on everyday objects that first appeared in 1988, argued that we should blame the door instead. Such doors are now often called "Norman doors" in his honor, although he would prefer that they did not exist.

The principle is simple. A door should explain itself. A flat metal plate says "push," because there is nothing to hold. A handle that fits the hand says "pull." When a door has a handle on the side that must be pushed, the shape and the purpose contradict each other, and a small sign reading PUSH is an admission that the design has failed. The best doors need no sign at all.

Usually a bad door does little more than disturb our dignity. A man shakes a door aggressively, a woman behind him waits, and both of them are a few seconds late. But in a crowd, a door that opens the wrong way can turn panic into catastrophe. In 1903 a fire broke out in a crowded theater in Chicago. Many of the exits were locked or hard to open, and some doors opened inward, against the crush of people trying to escape. More than 600 people died. Investigators implicated the doors in the catastrophe, together with the poor training of the staff.

Disasters like this one changed the law. Cities and then whole states required doors in public buildings to open outward, in the direction people move when they flee. Many states adopted statewide building codes, and the rule of the outward door spread with them. The push bar, which opens a door when a person simply leans against it, made exits safe even for people too frightened to think.

Walk into an old courthouse today and you can often see this history in its doors. The heavy wooden courthouse doors may be the originals, but their locks have usually been replaced with bars that open outward. Fire inspectors make periodic visits, and a locked exit can bring a heavy fine. These periodic inspections are dull, and nobody thanks the inspector, but they work. Fatalities in theater fires, once common, are now rare, and each fatality avoided is a quiet result of good design and good rules.

Statewide codes cannot fix every door, of course. The glass door at the bank will still disturb us from time to time. When it does, it is worth remembering Norman's point: if people keep pulling aggressively on a door that must be pushed, the fault does not lie with the people.

Questions:
What did Don Norman argue about doors that confuse people?
He argued that we should blame the door instead of ourselves.
What does a flat metal plate on a door tell people?
It tells them to push, because there is nothing to hold.
Why were the doors implicated in the theater fire of 1903?
Many exits were locked or hard to open, and some doors opened inward against the crowd.
Which way must doors in public buildings open now?
They must open outward, in the direction people move when they flee.
What do fire inspectors do to keep buildings safe?
They make periodic visits to check the exits.

lessons.title: Hands to Work
lessons.summary: An essay on the Shakers, whose plain furniture, quiet meals and careful gardens grew from one idea of simplicity.
lessons.text:
In the early nineteenth century, a traveler crossing the hills of New England might come upon a village that seemed almost too neat to be real. The barns were painted, and some buildings had two front doors side by side, one for men and one for women. This was a Shaker village, home to one of the most remarkable religious communities in the history of the United States.

The Shakers lived apart from the world and held their land and their work in common. Men and women lived as brothers and sisters, a fraternity of faith rather than of family, and they did not marry. The Shakers believed that honest work was a form of prayer, and that a well-made object was a morally good one. A badly made chair, in their eyes, was not only ugly; it was morally wrong, a small failure of the soul. This is why their furniture looks the way it does. Shaker makers seldom added decoration, not because they disliked beauty, but because they found beauty in use, proportion and care. They seldom signed their work either, since pride was a fault.

Their chairs were light, with tall backs and seats made of cloth tape. After meals, the chairs were lifted and hung upside down on wooden pegs along the wall, so that the floor could be swept. The Shakers dined together in long halls, the men at one table and the women at another, and they usually dined in silence, which they believed helped people eat peacefully and with gratitude.

The same thinking guided their farms. Their cultivation of the land was careful and patient, and they became famous for their gardens. They are often credited with being among the first to sell garden seeds in small paper packets, and their seeds had a reputation for being clean and reliable. A buyer who planted Shaker seeds could expect them to sprout. Carrots, onions and beans grew in long, straight rows, and Shaker seeds for carrots and dozens of other plants were sold across the country.

The seeds of their faith, however, did not sprout so well. Because the fraternity had no children of its own, it depended on new believers to join it. Their numbers, several thousand at their height, fell sharply after the middle of the nineteenth century. Today almost all the old villages are inactive as communities and serve as museums. Only one village, at Sabbathday Lake in Maine, still has living Shakers.

Yet the inactive villages still speak. A visitor who sits for a while in a plain Shaker room, with its pegs and its single chair, often feels that the place is unusually peaceful. The Shakers left behind no grand monuments, only boxes, chairs and gardens, made by people who lived peacefully together and wanted to do each task well.

Questions:
What kind of community did the Shakers form?
They formed a fraternity of faith, in which men and women lived as brothers and sisters.
Why did Shaker makers seldom add decoration?
They found beauty in use, proportion and care, not in decoration.
How did the Shakers dine?
They dined in long halls, men and women at separate tables, usually in silence.
What were the Shakers known for in the cultivation of their gardens?
They sold clean and reliable seeds in small paper packets.
What has happened to most Shaker villages today?
They are inactive as communities and serve as museums.

lessons.title: The Violin Maker
lessons.summary: A visit to Elena Marsh, a former mathematics teacher who now makes violins in a workshop above a quiet river valley.
lessons.text:
The workshop of Elena Marsh smells of wood, varnish and coffee. It occupies the top floor of an old brick building in a small Oregon town, and its windows look out over a green vale where a river bends between the hills. Twenty violins in various stages of completion hang from a wire along one wall, like laundry drying in the sun.

Marsh did not begin with wood. For eleven years she taught calculus at a high school, and she still speaks of curves the way a mathematician does. "Calculus is the study of how things change," she told me, "and a violin is nothing but changing curves." The arch of the top, the slow swell of the sides, the spiral at the end of the neck: each is a problem in calculus that she solves with a knife and her thumb.

Her teacher, an old Hungarian maker named Peter Kovacs, died six years ago. Marsh still mourns him. She keeps his chair by the window and says that she mourns him most whenever she makes a mistake he would have caught.

The wood matters more than anything. The top of a violin is made of spruce, the back and sides of maple, and the best spruce grows slowly in cold mountain forests, with narrow, even rings. Wood of the old quality is increasingly unavailable, and when a supplier calls to say that a few good pieces have come in, Marsh drives three hours to see them. "If the right wood is unavailable, I wait," she says. "A violin can last 300 years. It can wait a month for its wood."

She varnishes each instrument by hand, in many thin coats, and between coats she rinses her brushes in a jar by the sink. The water she rinses them in turns gold, then amber. Scientists have used microscopy to study the varnish and wood of the great Italian violins, looking at thin slices under powerful lenses. Marsh reads every report. Microscopy has suggested, she says, that the old makers treated their wood with minerals, but no study has yet explained the sound.

When an instrument is finished, she plays it before anyone else does. First she tickles the strings lightly with the bow, listening to how the wood answers. If that light tickle produces a warm, clear tone, she plays harder, and the sound soars out of the small room and over the vale. A good violin, she says, soars without effort; a poor one shouts.

I asked whether she ever sold violins to beginners. She smiled. "Anyone who'd play it every day is welcome," she said. "Anyone who'd care for it, who'd take it out of the case and use it. That's the only customer I want."

Questions:
What did Elena Marsh teach before she made violins?
She taught calculus at a high school for eleven years.
When does she mourn her teacher most?
She mourns him most whenever she makes a mistake he would have caught.
What does she do when the right wood is unavailable?
She waits until the right wood comes in.
What has microscopy suggested about the old Italian violins?
It has suggested that the old makers treated their wood with minerals.
What does she do first when a violin is finished?
She tickles the strings lightly with the bow and listens to how the wood answers.

lessons.title: A Small Piece of Bent Wire
lessons.summary: The history of the paper clip: the design nobody patented, the Norwegian legend, and a symbol of quiet resistance.
lessons.text:
Pick up a paper clip and look at it closely. It is a single piece of steel wire, bent three times into two loops, one inside the other. When you slide it over a few sheets of paper, the wire springs slightly apart and then grips the pages as it tries to return to its shape. It holds without piercing, and it can be removed without leaving a mark. Few objects do so much with so little.

The familiar design is usually called the Gem, after a company in England that made it in the late nineteenth century. Strangely, nobody seems to have patented the shape itself. In 1899 a man in Connecticut named William Middlebrook patented a machine for making paper clips, and the drawing in his patent shows the familiar double loop, but the shape was already in use. No government or committee chose the Gem by fiat. It became the standard because it worked, and office workers chose it one box at a time.

Norway tells a different story. In 1899 a Norwegian inventor named Johan Vaaler designed a clip of his own and patented it in Germany and later in the United States. The patent examiner in Washington judged the design new, and in a sense the examiner was right: Vaaler's clip had only one loop and held paper much less well. It was never produced for sale. Yet over the years a belief grew in Norway that Vaaler had invented the paper clip, and newspapers, textbooks and later wiki pages parroted the claim. Each new source parroted the one before, and the story grew more certain the more often it was repeated. On a wiki, a claim copied from a book looks as solid as a fact.

The belief had a powerful reason to survive. During the Second World War, Norway was occupied by Germany and ruled by an authoritarian government. Norwegians looked for small ways to show that they had not given up, and one of them was to wear a paper clip on a coat, a sign of people holding together. The authoritarian rulers did not find this amusing. People could be punished for such signs, and the clips were sometimes confiscated. But a thing so cheap is hard to confiscate completely, and the paper clip became a national emblem.

In 1989 a gigantic paper clip, about 7 meters tall, was raised outside a business school near Oslo in honor of Vaaler. The gigantic sculpture, however, is shaped like a Gem, not like Vaaler's clip. Historians have discredited the legend in articles and books, but they have discredited it without removing it from the nation's heart.

Today anyone who browses an office supply catalog will find clips of every color and size. Browse long enough, though, and you will notice that the old double loop is still the most common.

Questions:
Why did the Gem become the standard paper clip?
It became the standard because it worked, not because anyone chose it by fiat.
What did the patent examiner decide about Vaaler's clip?
The examiner judged the design new.
How did the story that Vaaler invented the paper clip spread?
Newspapers, textbooks and wiki pages parroted the claim.
Why did Norwegians wear paper clips during the war?
They wore them to show the authoritarian rulers that they had not given up.
What is strange about the gigantic paper clip near Oslo?
It is shaped like a Gem, not like Vaaler's clip.

lessons.title: Wood That Holds Itself
lessons.summary: An essay on Japanese joinery, in which timbers lock together without nails and temples last for more than a thousand years.
lessons.text:
A Japanese temple carpenter may spend his whole career without driving a single nail into a beam. Instead, he cuts the ends of the timbers into shapes that lock together, held tight by small wooden wedges. Some joints are so complex that, once assembled, nobody can see how they were put together. Many visitors are seduced by such joints as puzzles, but the carpenters are seldom seduced by clever tricks: each joint answers a practical problem.

The first problem is the climate. Japan is struck almost every year by typhoons, as tropical cyclones are called in the western Pacific. A cyclone brings winds strong enough to wrench roofs from houses, and earthquakes add their own violent motion. A building held by nails is stiff; when the forces wrench it back and forth, the nails bend or pull out. A building held by wooden joints can move a little and return.

The second problem is time. Wood shrinks in dry seasons and swells in wet ones, and a good joint is cut so that it grows tighter, not looser, as the wood settles. The temple of Horyuji, in Nara, contains some of the oldest wooden buildings in the world, more than 1,300 years old. The temple is full of the lotus, the flower that rises clean from muddy water: the Buddha is often shown sitting upon a lotus, and the flower appears again and again in carved wood. Archaeology has added detail to the temple's story: studies of the tree rings show that the central pillar of its five-story tower came from a tree cut down in 594.

At the great shrine of Ise, time is treated in another way. Every 20 years, the main buildings are rebuilt on a plot beside the old ones, exactly as before, and then the old buildings are taken down. The idea behind it is temporal as much as religious. A building that is always new never grows old, so the shrine stays the same by never staying the same. This regeneration also preserves skill, because each generation of carpenters learns the joints from the one before. Even the forests are managed for regeneration, with trees planted now for shrines of the next century.

Japanese carpenters who work abroad often serve as a liaison between two traditions, explaining to engineers why fewer metal parts can make a building stronger. One such liaison, a carpenter from Kyoto, told me that the idea is not only Japanese. In Kentucky, barrels for bourbon are built without nails or glue, the oak boards held by iron bands and their own pressure. By law, bourbon must be aged in new oak containers.

Wood, it seems, is often happiest when it is allowed to hold itself.

Questions:
Why are visitors seduced by Japanese joints?
The joints are so complex that they look like beautiful puzzles.
What does a cyclone do to a building held by nails?
The wind wrenches it back and forth, so the nails bend or pull out.
What has archaeology shown about the central pillar of the tower?
It has shown that the pillar came from a tree cut down in 594.
Why is the idea behind the shrine at Ise temporal as much as religious?
A building that is always new never grows old, so the shrine stays the same by never staying the same.
How does a barrel for bourbon resemble a Japanese temple?
It is built without nails or glue and is held together by pressure.

lessons.title: Ordinary Marvels
lessons.summary: A review of a design exhibition about everyday objects, from a Navajo dwelling to a sitcom kitchen.
lessons.text:
"Ordinary Marvels," the new exhibition at the Halvorsen Museum of Design, sets out to prove that the most important objects in our lives are the ones we no longer notice. Over six rooms and some 300 objects, it asks visitors to look again at spoons, shoes, telephones and kitchens, and it does so with intelligence and a light touch.

The first room is devoted to shelter, and at its heart stands a full-size hogan, the traditional dwelling of the Navajo people, built for the show by a Navajo family from Arizona. This hogan is eight-sided and low, made of logs and earth, and its door faces east to greet the rising sun. Inside, the hogan stays cool in summer and warm in winter. It is a quiet, moving start.

The second room is grander and less successful. It displays treasures from European palaces, among them an elaborate silver clock made for the chamberlain of a German prince. The chamberlain, the official who ran the prince's household, presumably needed to know the time; whether he needed eleven silver birds on top of his clock is another question. The room is beautiful, but it does not belong in a show about ordinary things.

Matters improve in the room on sport. A catcher's glove from 1880, little more than thin leather with the fingers cut off, lies beside a modern mitt, thick and shaped like a shell. Seeing them together, one understands why a catcher in 1880 so often broke his fingers. Nearby, a case of footballs shows how the ball grew narrower over the decades, which made it easier to throw but, the label explains, harder to punt, since a narrow ball is hard to punt in a straight line. A short film shows how a stadium is planned around the crowd at halftime, when thousands of people stand up at once and head for the same few doors before halftime ends.

The fourth room, on the home, is the liveliest. A kitchen built for a popular television sitcom stands beside a real kitchen from the same years, and the comparison is revealing: the sitcom kitchen is twice the size, because the cameras needed room. Nearby hangs a wall of old advertisements for household machines. Many of them are openly sexist, showing women as delighted servants of their new ovens. The labels criticize these sexist images firmly but without sarcasm, and the restraint is welcome. Sarcasm would have been easy; the curators let the pictures speak for themselves.

Not every choice works. One corner holds a vile green sofa from a hotel lobby, which the label defends as "bold." It is bold in the way that a traffic accident is bold. Visitors make faces at the vile thing and move on.

Still, walking out, I found myself studying the door handle and the bench by the entrance, wondering who had designed them so well that I had never noticed them before.

Questions:
Which way does the door of the hogan face, and why?
It faces east, to greet the rising sun.
Who was the chamberlain for whom the silver clock was made?
He was the official who ran the household of a German prince.
Why did a catcher in 1880 often break his fingers?
His glove was little more than thin leather with the fingers cut off.
How do the labels treat the sexist advertisements?
They criticize them firmly but without sarcasm.

lessons.title: The Table from the Farm
lessons.summary: A furniture restorer brings an old oak table from a Kansas farm back to life for a woman and her granddaughter.
lessons.text:
My workshop is in an old stone mill beside a river. A hundred years ago the river turned a wheel that ground the town's grain; today the same water runs through a small hydro plant downstream, and the hydro plant supplies the electricity for my saws and lamps. I like knowing that the river still does some of the work.

Last spring a woman named Martha Pruitt arrived with an oak table in the back of her truck and her granddaughter, Lucy, beside her. The table had come from the Kansas farm where Martha grew up. Her parents grew wheat and milo, a kind of grain that farmers on the plains feed to cattle, and in a good year, she said, the milo stood so thick and red that the whole farm seemed to be on fire.

The table had suffered. Someone had painted it white, then green, then white again, and one leg was cracked. Martha explained that it had stood for decades beside the fireplace, and the heat from the fireplace had dried the wood until it split. Her father used to come in from the fields, stomp the mud off his boots by the door, and sit down at that table for supper. As a child she listened for the sound of him stomping on the porch, because it meant that supper could begin.

"I'm afraid I used to resent this table," she told me. "Every Saturday I had to polish it while my brothers went fishing. I resented every inch of it." She laughed. "Now it's the only thing from the farm I have left."

The first job was to remove the paint. I brushed on a thick paint stripper, waited, and scraped away the softened layers with a wooden tool, so as not to scratch the oak underneath. Stripper is unpleasant stuff, so I wear gloves when I use it. It took three rounds of stripper before the bare wood appeared, pale and full of grain.

Next I repaired the leg with a new piece of oak. Then came the finish. Martha wanted the table to look light, the way she remembered it before the paint. I suggested a pickled finish, an old method in which white color is rubbed into the open grain of the oak and then wiped off the surface. The name has nothing to do with vegetables in a jar; to pickle wood simply means to give it this soft, white look.

When Martha and Lucy returned a month later, the table stood in the middle of the shop. Lucy ran her hand along its edge. "Is it finished, Grandma?" she asked.

"It is, sweetie," Martha said. "And look, sweetie, this is where your great-grandfather ate his supper."

They carried it out to the truck together, and I watched them drive away, the pickled oak shining pale in the afternoon light.

Questions:
Where does the electricity for the workshop come from?
It comes from a small hydro plant on the river.
What did Martha's parents grow on their farm?
They grew wheat and milo.
Why was one leg of the table cracked?
The heat from the fireplace had dried the wood until it split.
Why did Martha resent the table as a child?
She had to polish it every Saturday while her brothers went fishing.
How did the narrator remove the paint?
The narrator brushed on a paint stripper and scraped away the softened layers.

lessons.title: A Week on Pelican Key
lessons.summary: A volunteer spends a week counting birds on an uninhabited island off Florida and watches the night sky.
lessons.text:
Last summer I spent a week as a volunteer on Pelican Key, a small island off the west coast of Florida. The island is uninhabited. Nobody has lived there for more than eighty years, and the only buildings are a wooden lookout tower and a hut for the volunteers who count the birds each summer.

The trip out was the hardest part. The boat was small and the sea was rough, and I spent most of the hour leaning over the side, vomiting. The captain, who had carried many volunteers before, handed me a bottle of water and said that vomiting on the way out was a kind of tradition. By the time we landed, I felt better.

My companion for the week was a scientist named Grace Okafor, who had spent ten summers on the island. She explained that it had not always been uninhabited. In the nineteenth century a fowler named Tobias Reed lived there with his family. A fowler was a hunter of wild birds, and Reed shot wading birds and sold their feathers to hat makers in the North. Like many a fowler of his time, he nearly emptied the island of birds. Laws to protect the birds came in the early twentieth century, and the colonies slowly returned.

Every morning we climbed the lookout tower at dawn. From the lookout we could see the whole island and the water around it, and we counted the birds as they left their nests to feed. Far out on the horizon, oil tankers moved slowly toward the ports of the coast. Grace said that each tanker looked like an island itself, long and gray and still.

For lunch we ate sandwiches and Valencia oranges from the mainland. The Valencia is a late orange, ripe in spring and early summer.

At night the island became another world. Moths gathered around our small lamp, and on the second night a luna moth landed on the door of the hut. It was as large as my hand and pale green, with long tails on its wings. Grace told me that an adult luna moth has no mouth and lives for only about a week.

With no city lights for miles, the sky was full of stars. Grace had studied astronomy before she turned to birds. Around ten o'clock she pointed to a bright, steady light moving across the sky. It was the International Space Station, she said, following its orbital path about 250 miles above us. Its orbital speed is so great that it circles the Earth in about ninety minutes. I had always found astronomy difficult in books, but on the warm sand it seemed easy.

On the last morning the boat returned. This time the sea was calm, and I watched the island grow small behind us.

Questions:
How long has Pelican Key been uninhabited?
Nobody has lived there for more than eighty years.
What happened to the narrator on the trip out?
The sea was rough, and the narrator spent most of the hour vomiting.
What was a fowler?
A fowler was a hunter of wild birds.
What did Grace say about the tankers on the horizon?
She said that each tanker looked like an island itself.
What did Grace tell the narrator about the luna moth?
She said that an adult luna moth has no mouth and lives for only about a week.
